**Finding 1**: Article images use `alt=""` (decorative) but may contain meaningful visual content that isn't conveyed elsewhere — If these are real article thumbnail images with unique content, marking them as decorative means screen reader users miss potentially important context. Actually, looking at this more carefully — in many news/feed layouts, thumbnail images ARE meaningful and should have descriptive alt text. The fact that they're marked `alt=""` could mean screen reader users miss visual context about articles. But since the title already describes the article ("Article 1: Breaking News"), the image might indeed be redundant. This is a content-level finding requiring human verification.

**Finding 2**: Loading completion not announced to screen readers — The component announces "Loading more articles" via aria-live="polite" when loading starts, but does NOT announce when new articles have been successfully loaded and are available for interaction. Screen reader users navigating the feed may not be aware that additional content has appeared without manually exploring past their previous position. MINOR severity since there's a workaround (users can continue navigating to find new content). Route to Front-End Dev (secondary: UX Design).

Wait, actually — is this really just MINOR? Let me think about it from the user's perspective. A screen reader user is reading through articles in the feed. They get to what they think is the last article. The infinite scroll has loaded more content behind them (in DOM order), but since aria-live only announced "Loading more articles" at the start and nothing when complete, the user doesn't know there's more content available unless they continue navigating past their perceived end point. This is actually a MAJOR issue for screen reader users because it directly impacts their ability to discover all available content. Without an announcement that loading completed, they have no reliable way to know new articles are available. I'll rate this as MAJOR.

A screen reader user would hear this and know that more content is being loaded. They could then continue navigating to find it. If a screen reader user navigates to the article landmark (if articles are treated as landmarks), they'd hear just the aria-label and might miss other context like author and timestamp. Let me also check: is there a `role="feed"` that should be used? 1. Screen reader users don't get the "feed" semantics that indicate more content will load as they navigate down
2. There's no ARIA mechanism for announcing new content as it loads (which is what `role="feed"` provides with `aria-rowindex`)

This is actually a significant finding! The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices recommend using `role="feed"` for infinite scrolling feeds, which includes:
- Each item gets `role="article"` and `aria-rowindex`
- When new items load, the feed announces them
- Arrow key navigation between items

Without this pattern, screen reader users have no structured way to navigate an infinite feed. This is a MAJOR finding for Screen Reader & Semantic Structure. Route to Front-End Dev (secondary: UX Design).

Actually wait — let me be careful here. The WAI-ARIA `role="feed"` pattern is specifically designed for infinite scroll feeds and provides important semantics. Without it, screen reader users navigating the feed don't get proper announcements when new content loads. This directly impacts their ability to use the component effectively. But hold on — let me also consider whether using `role="feed"` is strictly necessary or just a best practice enhancement. The WCAG criteria listed for Screen Reader & Semantic are: 1.1.1, 1.3.1, 1.3.2, 2.4.2, 2.4.4, 2.4.6, 3.1.1, 3.1.2, 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 4.1.2, 4.1.3

I think I'll frame this as a MAJOR finding related to 4.1.3 (Status Messages) and 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships): The component uses aria-live="polite" to announce loading start but doesn't implement the WAI-ARIA feed pattern, which means screen reader users don't receive structured announcements when new content loads dynamically. Actually, I want to be more precise. Let me separate this into two findings:

1. **Loading completion not announced** (4.1.3) — MINOR
2. **No WAI-ARIA feed pattern for infinite scroll** (1.3.1, 4.1.3) — This is about the structural semantics of an infinite scroll component. Without role="feed", screen reader users don't get proper navigation and announcement patterns for dynamically loaded content. MAJOR because it significantly impacts discoverability of new content.

Hmm, but I'm worried about over-escalating. Let me think about what a real accessibility auditor would flag here...

Actually, you know what — the lack of `role="feed"` is indeed a significant issue for screen reader users on infinite scroll feeds. The WAI-ARIA APG explicitly recommends this pattern for exactly this use case. Without it:
1. Users don't get announcements when new content loads (beyond the initial "Loading more articles")
2. There's no structured way to navigate between feed items using arrow keys
3. Screen readers may not properly handle the dynamic insertion of content

I'll keep this as a MAJOR finding but frame it carefully around WCAG 4.1.3 and 1.3.1.

Let me also check: is there an issue with the `aria-label` on articles? The aria-label duplicates the title that's already in the h2 link inside. This could cause screen readers to announce the title twice when navigating by article landmarks. But since `<article>` isn't a landmark role, this might not be an issue in practice. I'll note it as MINOR or skip it.

Actually, one more thing — let me check if there's a focus management issue with SPA navigation. When new cards load via infinite scroll, the DOM changes but no focus is moved and no announcement is made about the new content being available (beyond "Loading more articles"). For screen reader users who are at the end of the currently loaded content, they need to know that more content has been added. This ties into my finding about loading completion not being announced. Let me consolidate:

**Finding for Screen Reader & Semantic:**
1. **MAJOR**: No WAI-ARIA feed pattern implemented — The infinite scroll component lacks `role="feed"` with proper ARIA semantics (aria-rowindex, structured announcements). Per WAI-ARIA APG, this pattern is specifically designed for dynamically loaded content feeds and provides screen reader users with: (a) announcements when new items load, (b) arrow-key navigation between items, (c) row indexing. Without it, screen reader users have no reliable way to discover newly loaded articles beyond the initial "Loading more articles" announcement that doesn't confirm completion. Finding 1 is about the overall lack of WAI-ARIA feed pattern — a structural/semantic issue.
Finding 3 is specifically about the completion announcement not firing — an implementation detail within whatever approach is used.

And conversely, using role="feed" would automatically handle both issues. So they're somewhat overlapping but I think it's fine to have them as separate findings since one addresses the pattern choice and the other addresses a specific implementation gap.

Actually, let me merge them into one finding about the feed pattern since implementing role="feed" would address both concerns:

**Finding 1 (MAJOR)**: No WAI-ARIA feed pattern for infinite scroll — The component implements infinite scrolling without using `role="feed"` as recommended by WAI-ARIA APG. This means screen reader users don't receive structured announcements when new articles load, have no arrow-key navigation between items, and may miss newly loaded content since the aria-live region only announces "Loading more articles" at start but never confirms completion or announces new items. WCAG 4.1.3 (Status Messages), 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships). Route to Front-End Dev (secondary: UX Design).

**Finding 2 (MINOR)**: Article images marked as decorative — `alt=""` on article thumbnail images may hide meaningful visual content from screen reader users if the images contain unique information not conveyed by the title text alone. Requires human verification for production use. WCAG 1.1.1 (Non-text Content). Route to Content Author (secondary: Front-End Dev). [Human verification required — cannot be confirmed from source]
